findings.impact: The approved test strategy cannot pass honestly against a real Git remote as written and could encourage a false claim that a patch-line CAS also guards production; this can stall delivery or obscure the reapproval required before production changes.
findings.text: Resolve the contradiction between per-destination CAS and the test claim that every destination write fails after production alone changes. If production moves after the last read but the isolated patch-line ref is unchanged, an expected-old-value CAS on that patch line can succeed; it does not compare production. Specify whether isolated patch-line writes are acceptable speculative work pending reapproval, or require an actual cross-ref guard, then make the tests assert the realizable contract. Include a real-remote race where only production changes immediately before an otherwise valid patch-line push, distinct from races that change the destination itself.

output.summary: The per-destination CAS contract and race tests now distinguish provisional patch work from guarded promotion.
Approved G1051 design for arbitrarily nested numeric release targets, equivalent trailing-zero aliases, and safely isolated patch and maintenance releases.

responses.adversary_design:4:1: fixed: permit an otherwise valid CAS to advance the isolated patch line provisionally when only production changes; distinguish it from a changed patch destination and require fresh approval and guarded promotion.
responses.review_design:4:1: fixed: explicitly allow provisional patch-line advancement after a separate production or source-goal race, require refreshed source/production approval before production or forward-port, and specify a real atomic source-verify/destination-update transaction or safe refusal when live source revocation must be enforced.

output.summary: Treat isolated patch-line advancement as provisional when only production or source-goal provenance races; destination CAS does not compare other refs. Require refreshed exact approval and guarded destination updates for promotion, and fail closed when policy requires live source verification but the remote lacks an actual cross-ref transaction.

Both reviewers raised material findings: the design overstates what destination-only compare-and-swap guarantees if production changes concurrently, including an unachievable test assertion and risk of advancing a patch line based on stale production. Both reopen design. There are no non-material notes to filter.

findings.impact: The engine can advance a patch line against stale production or revoked source provenance while reporting that the safety guard would have refused it.
findings.text: The revised race contract claims an external production move after a dispatch pre-read can result at worst in disposable speculative work, and that a stale patch-line update will fail its destination expected-SHA guard. That does not follow: if production advances after the last read but the patch-line ref itself remains unchanged, a CAS update of the patch-line ref against its expected old SHA succeeds. The same cross-ref gap applies if source goal approval/provenance changes while the patch-line destination stays put. Define what patch-line mutations remain authorized in that window, and do not claim a destination-only CAS detects changes to a separate production or goal ref. Either supply a genuinely atomic authorization mechanism across those refs or explicitly allow the isolated patch-line update and require a fresh, exact production/source approval and destination CAS before any production/forward-port action. Test the distinct-ref scenario, including a production move and a source-provenance revocation immediately before a patch-line update.

not: A ceremony framework: every mechanism must prevent a real failure worth its cost.
A second source of truth beside Git.
An engine that invents human decisions or acts without authority.
A deploy, CI or release-publishing tool: its release support is a branching strategy.
Inherently opinionated: it ships an opinionated default graph, but every opinion (graph, lenses, prompts, policy) can be customised by the project.
principles: Git is the store; state is visible and repairable by hand.
A small engine; the graph, prompts and policy belong to the project.
Human authority is explicit: approvals may be delegated, but decisions with big consequences go to the owner, batched.
Reviews are independent, and a finding must matter.

Guard against drift at both levels: from what a goal asked for, and from the project's original intent. A goal that departs from the project's intent is flagged when it is added, and the owner either changes the goal or amends the intent.
Prefer deleting to adding; keep prompts distilled.
intent.purpose: Let coding agents carry long-running repository work through durable, reviewable goals, so a developer can stop supervising without losing progress, priorities or control.
intent.serves: Developers who delegate project work to coding agents, and the agents doing it.

output.summary: The revised design accurately distinguishes provisional patch-line updates from independently changing production or source-goal refs, and requires guarded, freshly authorized promotion.

findings.text: The design requires an owner-approved insertion action before any patch member runs and a reviewed capability-gated policy activation, but explicitly leaves the insertion command, approved immutable-baseline input/preview and capability name unspecified. Existing release cut requires all members to close before cutting and accepts only integer names. Please specify the minimal actual insertion/approval and activation contracts needed to write real-CLI and remote-Git tests for isolated patch creation, completed-member refusal, production races, finish ordering and maintenance, without guessing implementation interfaces.

spec:
Support inserting a release between existing ZzzOps target releases, so a patch release can be planned and delivered without renumbering later work. The motivating example is targeting a patch release such as 2.1; target releases must no longer be restricted to integers. This is useful for shipping a ZzzOps fix as a patch while later releases are already planned.

Acceptance criteria:
- Let an owner insert, target and work toward an appropriately ordered release such as 2.1 alongside existing integer releases. Existing goals assigned to later releases remain assigned to those releases unless explicitly changed. A patch release can use the existing release workflow and gates.
- Define and validate release identifiers and their ordering explicitly. Avoid treating version-like identifiers as floating-point numbers: for example, 2.10 and 2.1 must not silently collapse into the same identifier. The supported identifier grammar and how it relates to actual semantic versions are design choices to surface to the owner if not already decided.
- Integrate the identifier through the actual engine, goal schema, CLI, default workflow, release and branch handling, scheduling, display, validation, docs and compatibility boundaries wherever relevant. Do not assume a particular release-branch naming scheme without checking existing policy.
- Preserve existing integer release data and goal histories; do not silently reorder, rewrite or repurpose existing releases or production branches. Analyze how existing repositories and in-flight goals adopt the new version; report unrelated broken migrations for a separate goal rather than expanding scope to repair them.
- Cover identifier parsing and ordering, insertion with later targets already present, scheduling, release cutting and completion, compatibility with existing integer goals, invalid and ambiguous input, branch/CLI behavior and mixed engine versions using realistic local Git/remote fixtures. Run focused real-engine checks first, followed by appropriate integration checks.

Constraints: ZzzOps release support is a branching strategy, not an automatic deployment or package-publishing service. Respect existing owner approvals and policy choices. Do not create a real release, change production branches, publish artifacts or change other goals' release assignments as part of capturing this goal.

Owner clarification: releases can always be inserted by adding another dot-delimited numeric component. For example, after 2.1 exists, insert 2.0.1 before it, then insert 2.0.0.1 before 2.0.1: 2 < 2.0.0.1 < 2.0.1 < 2.1. Support arbitrarily nested finite component sequences rather than imposing a fixed version depth. Trailing-zero forms representing the same value, such as 2 and 2.0, are equivalent; 2.1 and 2.10 remain distinct. Design and test ordering, canonical identity, branch naming, insertion, compatibility and safe patch-line ancestry at nested depths.
title: Allow inserting patch target releases between planned releases
